---
title: "Beta diversity"
format: html
editor: visual
---

Beta diversity quantifies how different the taxonomic composition of two samples is. It is calculated as a distance (or dissimilarity) between each pair of samples. Several distance metrics exist, and each of them emphasises different aspects of the communities: the abundant OTUs, the rare OTUs, or only their presence or absence. The choice of the metric can change the interpretation of the data, as shown below.

This section documents how to calculate distance matrices with three metrics (Bray-Curtis, Aitchison and Jaccard), how to visualise them with a Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA), and how to test differences between groups of samples with PERMANOVA and the homogeneity of group dispersions. To follow the example presented on this page directly on your computer, download the script `020_beta_diversity.R` and the example data by clicking the buttons below. Alternatively, you may copy the codes below into your own script, and use your own data.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
library(downloadthis)
library(phyloseq)
library(vegan)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggpubr)
library(dplyr)
load("../../RData/ITS/otu_BLAST_clean.RData")
```

To get started, load the OTU table filtered with BLAST (see [BLAST filtering](../otu-tables/filter/BLAST.qmd)), and set the seed for the rarefaction and the permutation tests. We also order the land uses from agriculture to the old forest, for the plots and tables.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Load the cleaned OTU table from previous scripts
load("RData/ITS/otu_BLAST_clean.RData")
```

```{r}
set.seed(100)

sample_data(otu_BLAST_clean)$Land_use <- factor(
  sample_data(otu_BLAST_clean)$Land_use,
  levels = c("Conventional agriculture", "Organic agriculture", "Grassland",
             "Oak", "Old Ref"))
```

## Data transformation

Metabarcoding data are compositional: the number of reads does not reflect the total abundance of the fungi in the soil, only the relative abundances within a sample can be compared. The data also contain a long tail of rare OTUs: a few OTUs are very abundant and most are rare. The data must therefore be transformed before calculating distances (see also [Rarefaction & normalization](../otu-tables/rare-norm.qmd)).

### Rarefied data and Hellinger transformation

As in [Alpha diversity](alpha-div.qmd#rarefaction), we start from the data rarefied to 1011 reads (same seed, so the same rarefied table).

```{r}
#| message: false
otu_table_rarefy <- rarefy_even_depth(otu_BLAST_clean, sample.size = 1011,
                                      replace = FALSE, rngseed = 100,
                                      verbose = FALSE)
nsamples(otu_table_rarefy)
ntaxa(otu_table_rarefy)

# Check: all samples should have 1011 reads
summary(sample_sums(otu_table_rarefy))
```

The Hellinger transformation is the square root of the relative abundances [@legendre2001]. Dividing by the sample total converts the counts to relative abundances, and the square root gives less weight to the few very abundant OTUs (it stabilises the variance).

```{r}
otu_table_hel <- transform_sample_counts(otu_table_rarefy,
                                         function(x) sqrt(x / sum(x)))
```

### Non-rarefied data for the Aitchison distance

The Aitchison distance is calculated on the non-rarefied data (all 89 samples). `vegan::vegdist()` needs a matrix with the samples as rows, so we extract the OTU table from the `phyloseq` object. We also keep the metadata of the samples for the plots and tests below.

```{r}
otu_mat <- as(otu_table(otu_BLAST_clean), "matrix")
if (taxa_are_rows(otu_BLAST_clean)) otu_mat <- t(otu_mat) # samples = rows
dim(otu_mat)

meta_rare <- data.frame(sample_data(otu_table_rarefy)) # 87 samples
meta_all  <- data.frame(sample_data(otu_BLAST_clean))  # 89 samples
```

## Distance matrices

Each distance metric emphasises different aspects of the communities:

-   **Bray-Curtis**: abundance-based, dominated by the abundant OTUs. Here it is calculated on the Hellinger-transformed rarefied data.
-   **Aitchison**: the Euclidean distance between centred log-ratio (CLR) transformed abundances. It is designed for compositional data [@gloor2017], and does not need rarefied data. The log of 0 is not defined, so a small constant (pseudocount) is added to all counts.
-   **Jaccard**: presence-absence only (`binary = TRUE`), the abundances are ignored. Calculated on the rarefied data.

Other metrics exist, e.g. UniFrac, which uses the phylogenetic relationships between OTUs. It is not available for ITS, which cannot be aligned across all fungi.

```{r}
# Bray-Curtis dissimilarities on the Hellinger-transformed data
dist_bray <- phyloseq::distance(otu_table_hel, method = "bray")
head(dist_bray)

# Aitchison distances on the non-rarefied data, with a pseudocount of 1
dist_ait <- vegdist(otu_mat, method = "aitchison", pseudocount = 1)
head(dist_ait)

# Jaccard distances on the rarefied data (presence-absence)
dist_jac <- phyloseq::distance(otu_table_rarefy, method = "jaccard",
                               binary = TRUE)
head(dist_jac)
```

::: callout-note
The tutorial of the course uses the `"robust.aitchison"` distance, which only uses the non-zero counts instead of adding a pseudocount (see [Rarefaction & normalization](../otu-tables/rare-norm.qmd)). Both are valid. With a pseudocount, absent OTUs and OTUs with very few reads get similar values, which is important to interpret the PCoA below.
:::

## Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA)

A distance matrix contains one value for each pair of samples (87 samples: 3741 pairs), too many to look at. An ordination such as the Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA) summarises the distances in a few axes, so that similar samples are close to each other in the plot. `phyloseq::ordinate()` runs the PCoA with `ape::pcoa()`.

```{r}
pcoa_bray <- ordinate(otu_table_hel, method = "PCoA", distance = dist_bray)
pcoa_ait  <- ordinate(otu_BLAST_clean, method = "PCoA", distance = dist_ait)
pcoa_jac  <- ordinate(otu_table_rarefy, method = "PCoA", distance = dist_jac)

# Proportion of the variation explained by the first axes
head(pcoa_bray$values$Relative_eig)
head(pcoa_ait$values$Relative_eig)
head(pcoa_jac$values$Relative_eig)
```

### Plot

The three PCoA plots use the same code, so we write it in a function. `plot_pcoa()` draws the samples on the first two axes, coloured by site, with an ellipse for each land use.

```{r}
# Colours for each site and each land use
site_col <- c("Conv_agri" = "bisque", "Org_agri" = "bisque3",
              "Grass" = "orange",
              "Oak_20" = "darkolivegreen1", "Oak_28" = "darkolivegreen2",
              "Oak_33" = "darkolivegreen3", "Oak_44" = "palegreen3",
              "Oak_51" = "darkolivegreen4", "Oak_54" = "darkolivegreen",
              "Oak_ref" = "turquoise4")
land_use_col <- c("Conventional agriculture" = "bisque",
                  "Organic agriculture" = "bisque3",
                  "Grassland" = "orange",
                  "Oak" = "darkolivegreen2",
                  "Old Ref" = "turquoise4")

#   - physeq: the phyloseq object used for the distances (for the metadata)
#   - pcoa: the result of ordinate()
#   - title: the title of the plot
plot_pcoa <- function(physeq, pcoa, title) {
  # Sample scores on the first two axes, with the metadata of the samples
  scores <- plot_ordination(physeq, pcoa, justDF = TRUE)
  # Variation explained by the first two axes, for the axis labels
  var_expl <- round(100 * pcoa$values$Relative_eig[1:2], 1)

  ggplot(scores, aes(x = Axis.1, y = Axis.2)) +
    stat_ellipse(aes(fill = Land_use), geom = "polygon", alpha = 0.4) +
    geom_point(aes(colour = SiteID), size = 2.5) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = site_col, breaks = names(site_col)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = land_use_col) +
    labs(title = title,
         x = paste0("Axis 1 (", var_expl[1], "%)"),
         y = paste0("Axis 2 (", var_expl[2], "%)"),
         colour = "Site", fill = "Land use") +
    coord_fixed() +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
}
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
p_pcoa_bray <- plot_pcoa(otu_table_hel, pcoa_bray,
                         "Bray-Curtis (Hellinger, rarefied)")
p_pcoa_bray
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
p_pcoa_ait <- plot_pcoa(otu_BLAST_clean, pcoa_ait,
                        "Aitchison (CLR, non-rarefied)")
p_pcoa_ait
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
p_pcoa_jac <- plot_pcoa(otu_table_rarefy, pcoa_jac,
                        "Jaccard (presence-absence, rarefied)")
p_pcoa_jac
```

### Compare the distance metrics

```{r}
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 6
p_pcoa_all <- ggarrange(p_pcoa_bray, p_pcoa_ait, p_pcoa_jac,
                        ncol = 3, common.legend = TRUE, legend = "right")
p_pcoa_all
```

In the three PCoAs, the first axis separates the agricultural sites from the grassland and the forests: this is the largest difference in the fungal communities. Conventional and organic agriculture overlap. With Bray-Curtis and Jaccard, the old reference forest (Oak_ref) is clearly separated from the oak plantations (only one sample of Oak_51 lies close to it). With Aitchison, the samples of the reference forest are spread along the second axis, and their ellipse overlaps with the plantations.

The metrics therefore lead to different conclusions about how similar the plantations are to the reference forest. Which one to use? The Jaccard distances only use presence-absence, and show the same separation as Bray-Curtis: the plantations and the reference forest differ in which OTUs are present, not only in their abundances. With the Aitchison distance, a pseudocount is added to all counts before the log-ratio transformation, so absent OTUs and OTUs with very few reads get similar values. This can blur the differences caused by OTUs that are present in one group and absent in the other.

## PERMANOVA

The PCoA shows the patterns, but does not test them. The permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) tests whether the centroids (multivariate means) of groups of samples differ [@anderson2001]. `vegan::adonis2()` calculates a pseudo-F ratio, similar to the F ratio of an ANOVA, and compares it with the values obtained after randomly permuting the samples between groups. The null hypothesis is H~0~: the centroids of all groups are equivalent.

### Site and land use

We first test site and land use in the same model, each one after the other (`by = "margin"`).

```{r}
set.seed(100)
adonis2(dist_bray ~ SiteID + Land_use, data = meta_rare,
        permutations = 999, by = "margin")
```

Land use has 0 degrees of freedom and no F value. Why? Look at the metadata:

```{r}
table(meta_rare$SiteID, meta_rare$Land_use)
```

Each site belongs to a single land use: `SiteID` is nested within `Land_use`. Once the sites are in the model, land use cannot explain anything more: the two variables are redundant. We therefore test each variable alone.

```{r}
set.seed(100)
adonis2(dist_bray ~ SiteID, data = meta_rare, permutations = 999)

set.seed(100)
adonis2(dist_bray ~ Land_use, data = meta_rare, permutations = 999)
```

Both site and land use are significantly associated with the composition of the fungal communities (p = 0.001, the smallest p-value possible with 999 permutations). Sites explain 43% of the variation (R^2^ = 0.43), land use 30% (R^2^ = 0.30). Sites explain more because they include the land use and the differences between the sites of the same land use (e.g., plantations of different ages).

With `by = "terms"`, the variables are tested in sequence: each term only gets the variation not explained by the terms before it. Land use first, then the differences between the sites of the same land use:

```{r}
set.seed(100)
adonis2(dist_bray ~ Land_use + SiteID, data = meta_rare,
        permutations = 999, by = "terms")
```

Land use explains 30% of the variation, and the sites explain another 13% within land uses: 30% + 13% = the 43% explained by the sites alone.

### Compare the distance metrics

Is the effect of land use the same with the three distance metrics? The Aitchison distances include the two samples removed by rarefaction, so they use the metadata of all samples.

```{r}
set.seed(100)
adonis2(dist_ait ~ Land_use, data = meta_all, permutations = 999)

set.seed(100)
adonis2(dist_jac ~ Land_use, data = meta_rare, permutations = 999)
```

Land use is significant with the three metrics, and explains a similar part of the variation with Bray-Curtis (R^2^ = 0.30) and Aitchison (R^2^ = 0.28), but less with Jaccard (R^2^ = 0.19). Presence-absence gives the same weight to all OTUs: the many rare OTUs, found by chance in only a few samples, add variation that is not related to land use.

### Soil properties

We can also test the effect of soil properties. Samples of the same land use are not independent. With the `strata` argument, the samples are only permuted within each land use (similar to a random factor in mixed models), so the test asks whether pH and phosphate explain the composition within land uses.

```{r}
set.seed(100)
adonis2(dist_bray ~ pH + PO4, data = meta_rare, permutations = 999,
        by = "margin", strata = meta_rare$Land_use)
```

Both pH (R^2^ = 0.13) and phosphate (R^2^ = 0.03) are significant (p = 0.001).

::: callout-note
`strata` only changes how the samples are permuted, not the R^2^, which is still calculated on the total variation. pH differs strongly between land uses, so part of its R^2^ may also reflect the effect of land use.
:::

## Homogeneity of group dispersions

Homogeneity of the dispersions is not an assumption of PERMANOVA, but it affects its results: a significant PERMANOVA can be caused by differences in the spread of the samples within groups (dispersion), not only by different centroids. `vegan::betadisper()`, a multivariate analogue of Levene's test [@anderson2006], calculates the distance of each sample to the centroid of its group. We then test whether these distances differ between groups.

```{r}
# Bray-Curtis
disp_bray <- betadisper(dist_bray, meta_rare$SiteID)
anova(disp_bray)

# Aitchison
disp_ait <- betadisper(dist_ait, meta_all$SiteID)
anova(disp_ait)
```

### Plot

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
# Distance to the centroid of each sample, for both metrics
disp_df <- rbind(
  data.frame(meta_rare[, c("SiteID", "Land_use")],
             distance = disp_bray$distances, metric = "Bray-Curtis"),
  data.frame(meta_all[, c("SiteID", "Land_use")],
             distance = disp_ait$distances, metric = "Aitchison"))
disp_df$metric <- factor(disp_df$metric, levels = c("Bray-Curtis", "Aitchison"))

# Order the sites by land use for the plot
disp_df$SiteID <- factor(disp_df$SiteID,
                         levels = unique(disp_df$SiteID[order(disp_df$Land_use,
                                                              disp_df$SiteID)]))

p_disp <- ggplot(disp_df, aes(x = SiteID, y = distance)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = Land_use), outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(size = 1, width = 0.1, height = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = land_use_col) +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Distance to the site centroid", fill = "Land use") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
p_disp
```

The dispersions differ significantly between sites with both metrics (Bray-Curtis: F = 19.9, p \< 0.001; Aitchison: F = 12.0, p \< 0.001). The boxplots show that the agricultural samples have a lower dispersion than the other sites: their communities are more homogeneous (with Aitchison, also the youngest plantation, Oak_20). The reference forest has one of the highest dispersions. Part of the significant PERMANOVA may therefore be due to differences in dispersion, although the PCoA also shows a clear separation of the groups.

### Without the agricultural sites

Do the other sites have similar dispersions? We remove the agricultural samples from the distance matrix and test again.

```{r}
keep <- !meta_rare$Land_use %in% c("Conventional agriculture",
                                   "Organic agriculture")
dist_bray_noagri <- as.dist(as.matrix(dist_bray)[keep, keep])
disp_bray_noagri <- betadisper(dist_bray_noagri, meta_rare$SiteID[keep])
anova(disp_bray_noagri)
```

Without the agricultural sites, the dispersions still differ between sites (F = 3.6, p = 0.003), but much less: the differences in dispersion are mainly due to the agricultural sites. Among the other sites, Oak_51 and Oak_ref are the most dispersed.

## Exercise

Is there an effect of age on the composition of the fungal communities in the forests (oak plantations and old reference forest)?

Hints:

-   Keep only the samples of the land uses "Oak" and "Old Ref", e.g. with `subset_samples()` on `otu_table_hel`, then calculate the Bray-Curtis distances again.
-   The column `Age` of the metadata gives the age of the forest (years).
-   Is age confounded with site? How many sites are there for each age?
